Fifteen days, mapped: the coverage, who acted, and the documented ties

Top right, each dot is one piece on the story. Below it, each row is one actor and each chip one dated act. At left, each line is a documented tie between an actor and a company, a funder or a group: a contribution, a post held, a grant, an official act. Both slices repeat the same companies, funders and people at their left; a dashed box names an actor whose own row is in another slice. The ties are mapped outward from Anthropic and Open Philanthropy; Nvidia's are added where the same kind of record was searched (the note at the foot lists them), and each group's heading gives the rule for who is drawn. The figure sets these records side by side; it does not say one caused another.

THREE NEWSPAPERS
Background: The New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times cover chips and China.
No document here shows who their confidential intelligence sources are. Singapore's ministry denied the Journal's Oct 30 account in a statement timed the same day.
BYLINES WITH A TIE ON RECORD
No document here shows whether a tie shaped any of the five pieces. All 873 names in the bylines of the saved pages were looked up; five have a tie on record (three of them to the Tarbell Center). A reporter or columnist without one is not drawn, however often quoted.
ANALYSTS QUOTED OR POSTING
Background: Chris McGuire, now at the Council on Foreign Relations, "crafted and implemented" the Biden administration's chip export controls at the NSC, his biography says. CNAS published on chip smuggling in 2025.
No document here shows who, if anyone, prompted the posts or quotes. Drawn: 16 of the 280 analysts, experts and research groups quoted: those with a tie on record to Anthropic, Open Philanthropy or Nvidia, their own or through the organisation where they hold a post.
SENATE
Background: Democrats sen. Schumer was an original cosponsor of the GAIN AI Act on chip exports.
No document here shows any contact between a senator and the reporters or their sources.
The New York Times what it reported, from its own pages unless a chip says otherwise
Sources not public. Its reporters' names, where a saved page carries them, were looked up in the fellowship and staff records held: no record. Nothing else about them was examined
U.S. intelligence surveilled Alice Huang
A memo says China's spy agency recruited her
A Chinese firm was cleared to assemble Nvidia chips
Rubio oversaw the memo
Reports that a Commerce Department investigation of Megaspeed "came to a sudden halt late last year" and was "transferred to the Justice Department", after Nvidia's general counsel emailed the investigators in August 2025. It says the transfer was "to avoid any potential compromise" of the investigation, that Justice "is conducting a criminal inquiry into Megaspeed", and that "it is not clear if other factors contributed"
Reports that the president was told aboard Air Force One in May, by Rubio, of the intelligence on Huang, which "contradicts the president's assertion" that he had not known then; the White House "disputed the reporting", it says, "without elaborating"
A second relationship, with a subordinate. Reports that Bessent "confronted" Lutnick at the White House over Megaspeed, as "described by people briefed on it"; a Commerce spokeswoman denies the conversation took place
The Wall Street Journal what it reported, from its own page saved by hand and from copies its licensed partners carry
Sources not public. Its reporters' names, where a saved page carries them, were looked up in the fellowship and staff records held: no record. Nothing else about them was examined
Reports that officials in the U.S., Singapore and Taiwan "have grown concerned" that an executive close to Huang "is a Chinese intelligence source", citing people familiar with the matter (Singapore denied the account in a statement timed the same day)
Reports that the board "is preparing to oust" Huang and "to meet as soon as today to determine his future", citing people familiar with the matter
Financial Times what it reported, from its own page
Its report of Sep 4, 2025 that Anthropic would stop selling AI services to groups majority-owned by Chinese entities cited "an Anthropic executive familiar with the matter", as Bloomberg Law relays it. No record here shows who the sources of its Nov 6 report were
Sources not public. Its reporters' names, where a saved page carries them, were looked up in the fellowship and staff records held: no record. Nothing else about them was examined

A tie is a dated record, not a motive.
No document here shows that any tie prompted a report, a post or a statement. Each line ends at a person or a body, never at an act; the acts sit on the calendar at right.
13 of the 27 members drawn received an AnthroPAC contribution; 14 did not, and they pressed the matter too. The PAC paid 81 candidates in all, 38 Democrats and 43 Republicans. Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom are themselves among the seven companies that agreed to buy Anthropic stock. Employees' gifts are their own money: 154 of the 535 sitting members received one from someone who gave Anthropic as employer, 19 of the 27 drawn here. The same count for Nvidia's employees is worded in each member's row. Ties the source article asserts but no document here supports are not drawn.

Reading it: the dots count pieces, not readers; a piece is placed on the first day a saved Techmeme or Memeorandum page lists it (pages for 9 am, noon, 4 pm, 8 pm and 11 pm Eastern each day), and 9 more pieces seen only on undated pages are left out. A piece counts as on the story when its address or listed headline names Huang, Megaspeed or Alice Huang, tells of the spy affair without naming them, or names Nvidia with a word of the affair (resign, board, inquiry, chief, successor and the like). That rule was applied by script, not by reading each piece, to the 2,465 links on those pages that name Huang, Nvidia, Megaspeed or the spy story. The 231 links the rule left out were then read, 150 of them by an independent auditor and the rest by the builder: 20 are plainly on the story and are counted with it, and 16 could not be settled from their headlines. Left out are 117 links on the wider fallout (export controls, the Commerce secretary, the share price, Anthropic's stock offering) and 94 others; a counted piece may name Huang for another reason. Every link, its class and each reading is published with the figure's tables. They are sorted into the three kinds by site and by the section named in the page address, not by reading them. A chip is one dated act, worded from a saved report; it starts on its day, and a long one may run on over empty days to its right. View counts are those shown when the posts were saved on Nov 12. An act is placed on the day its source gives or, failing that, the day the source was published: those chips have a dashed left edge, and the act itself may be earlier. Where one chip holds two acts of a day and only one is dated by its report, the edge is solid and the words say which. Where a chip rests on one outlet's account of another's report, it says so. Grant figures are awards, not payments traced to a bank. An announced ad is not proof that it ran. Nvidia's board said on Nov 8 it had "no reason to believe" national security or company secrets were compromised, and NBC reported on Nov 12 that Alice Huang's "precise role" remained unclear. Counts of who is named or quoted are counts of articles, each counted once: the 1,086 pages saved by the first search and the 229 saved since (the papers' own articles, saved by hand or in a licensed copy, a few transcripts and a company filing) are 1,236 articles once copies of one article are joined, and 1,154 of them are counted. Two pages are one article when they have the same address or when a reader judged them so: every two pages that share 25 or more seven-word runs making up a fifth of the shorter were opened by a reader from another model family (504 pairs over six readings; six more were decided by the builder under a stated rule, and the table says which. Of the 510, 87 are the same article, as a syndicated or licensed copy with its lead kept, a later version at one address or two snapshots of a live page, and 423 are different, such as a statement and the articles quoting it, or a later dispatch with a new lead; four more could not be read, being block pages that are not counted). Copies that share less than that are not listed, so the number of articles can still be a little high. A page's day is the day of its first publication where the page shows one, and otherwise the day of the version saved, read as a U.S. Eastern day from the page's own stamp (50 pages whose metadata and text carry none, or carry one the printed stamp contradicts, were read in their saved copy). A page is not counted when that day is after Nov 12 (57 pages) or before Oct 29 (13, background pages), when the saved copy is a block or error page (6) or holds nothing at all (2), or when it is a reference page or an image (8). For 25 pages whose first extraction had missed the article, its text was taken again from the saved HTML (four of them a second time, after a reading found paragraphs missing or other lines among them); 98 counted pages are still held only in part (a headline and description, a teaser, an excerpt, the opening before a subscription barrier, a live page whose entries are collapsed or load only on request): 58 that the readers of the pages had listed, and 40 more found on Nov 16: 35 among the 248 counted pages that show a sign of a barrier or hold a short text, which readers went through, and five live pages that later readings found among the longer pages. A page is whole when all of the listed page's own piece is saved, whatever it quotes or links to. A longer page that shows no sign of a barrier was not read again for this: every counted page with a collapse mark in its text was read, and every saved page whose HTML holds a live-blog record was compared with its text; a live page saved by hand as PDF cannot be checked that way. On four live pages the saved HTML held 174 entries that the text read lacked, and they were added to it. One of them is a four-day live page of general news: an article is counted for a member when its text names the member anywhere, so there, as in any round-up, the name can stand in an entry about something else; the four members it names only for other news carry a note beside their count. On six pages a table or a photo caption of the piece, which the extraction from the saved HTML had left out, was added to the text read, after a search of every page's HTML for a member's name missing from its text (a member counts as named when the name stands in the piece's own table or caption), and on two pages a short paragraph or passage; other photo captions and some small parts of a piece (a subheading, a credit, a short sentence) are not in the text read, and that search does not find other passages an extraction may have lost. On four pages saved by hand as PDF, 21 lines of prose that the cleaning of the text had dropped at page breaks were put back. The ten people at three or four articles (eight members and two public voices) were each read for whether those articles are separate reports, and all have three. Two senators reach three only through a report saved on Nov 16 that the record had pointed to and the saved pages lacked: one through a piece the aggregators listed on Nov 12 (a paper's live page had repeated its own article, leaving two reports), one through a report that a reader had quoted under a blog post. The saved pages are about half of the pieces listed, so a member whose reports were not saved can be missing from these counts. Members of Congress drawn are every current member named in three or more of those 1,154 articles, as separate reports, for something said or done about the matter in these days, and one senator (Cotton) whom they name that often for a letter on Megaspeed a year earlier; each one's count is in their row. Ten others named that often are not drawn, because the pages name them for other things: a leadership vote, a lost election, a race still being counted, an impeachment bid, a missed vote and other inquiries. The names searched came from the readings of the pages, so on Nov 16 every sitting member's name was also searched as a whole name over the counted articles and over the headlines of the listed pieces that could not be saved (about half of the pieces listed were saved): 60 more members are named, none in more than two. The count for every name searched is published with the figure's tables. The articles counted quote 280 analysts, experts and research groups (a person or firm written two ways is counted once). Each was looked up in the records held. On Nov 15, and on Nov 16 for the names added since, the names not drawn were searched again as whole names in the 85 tables of the four evidence sets: 1,022 names of two to four words among the analysts and the bylines (people's names, and a few firms and labels of the same form), and 36 other firm names and one-word names among the analysts; 81 entries (bylines that are an agency, a label or an address, and analyst labels under four letters) were left out of that pass. The 16 drawn each have a remark of these days and a tie on record to Anthropic, Open Philanthropy or Nvidia: their own (a fellowship, research support, a past post, a seat on an advisory council) or that of the organisation where they hold a post (an award to it, a paid business relationship, a paper it was commissioned to write); each row says which, and an award to an organisation is not a payment to the person. At a university an award counts for a person only where the record names that person's own unit. Not drawn: 4 people at universities whose only award on record names the university as a whole, or another researcher there; 8 for whom the record is a remark or report not shown to be of these days, a past post at a group funded only later, a grant from another company, a grant to their group from an investor in Anthropic, or an invitation to speak with no post or payment on record; 2 the look-up could not tell apart from others of the same name; 17 entries that are one of the banks below or its analysts; and the other 233, for whom no record was found. No tie is implied for anyone not drawn. Bank analysts, and investors quoted for their view of the shares, are not drawn, whatever their ties; three investors, Ackman, Maguire and Conway, are drawn among the public voices, under that row's rule of three articles. Quartz reported on Sep 4, 2026, citing unnamed sources of Bloomberg's, that Anthropic was nearing a credit facility before its share sale, and named 17 banks in it, four of them also leading the sale; the report says the details could still change. Analysts, or executives in office, of 11 of those banks are quoted on the saved pages. The banks' business with Nvidia was not looked up. Two quoted investors are described on the pages as a shareholder and a short seller of Nvidia. The pages counted carry 948 bylines, counting a name once for each outlet it appears at: 873 different names, 75 of them agencies or not a person's name. These are the bylines of the pages counted, those of the first search and those saved since; a page saved as an actor's own original is cited on that actor's chip and its byline is not counted here. Each was looked up in the fellowship and staff records held and, on Nov 15 or 16, in the whole-name search. Five have a tie on record and are drawn: Perlo and Hashim from the records held, Kubinec from his own bio at The Dispatch, Mowshowitz and Schneider from pages saved on Nov 15 (the first look-up had missed both). Two more have a record of another kind and no tie is drawn: a congressional fellow of the 2021 cohort of a programme that Open Philanthropy funded in 2025 (the record shows no overlap), and a reporter named on the page of a CSET event. A CSET staff member's byline on a CSET release of 2025 is no longer counted, because that page is dated before these days (he also wrote CSET's two releases of Nov 10 and 11, which are drawn in CSET's row). For three the tables hold the name and nothing ties it to the reporter. Pages that could not be saved were not checked. The lists of the names looked up are not published, because most name people for whom nothing was found; the counts and the rules are. "No AnthroPAC contribution on file" means none in the PAC's filings with the Federal Election Commission for Jun 29 to Sep 30, 2026. A line that says no gift from a company's employees means that no FEC line for Jan 2025 to Oct 14, 2026 gives that company as the donor's employer to a committee tied to the member; it is not proof that no employee gave. Lines dated after Oct 14, 2026 are not in the FEC records read here: where a committee must file a post-general report (its books close Nov 23), that report is due on Dec 3, 2026; other committees follow their own schedules. No line of a sitting member's campaign committee dated after Sep 30, 2026 is on file yet from either company's employees. Gifts made through the conduits ActBlue and WinRed after that day are on file only as the conduits' own lines (26 from people who gave Anthropic as employer, $2,741; 350 for Nvidia, $14,345) and are not counted until the recipient's own report shows them; among the members drawn they name only 2 Nvidia lines ($15) for the committee of Sen. Elizabeth Warren. A committee is tied to a member when it is the member's campaign committee, a leadership PAC the member sponsors, or a joint fundraising committee whose statement of organisation lists that member's committee and no other sitting member's; money given to a joint committee is shared with its other participants (a party committee, a PAC), and the FEC lines do not show how much reached the member's own campaign. Joint committees of several members are listed with the figure's tables and attributed to no one. An employee's gift is counted from an FEC line on which the donor gave the company as employer, to a committee tied to the member; donors are counted, not named, and the two companies are counted by one rule, though not from equally deep records, as the next sentences say. Both companies' lines come from the FEC's bulk file of itemised individual contributions for the 2026 cycle, downloaded Nov 13, 2026 (it carries whole dollars), plus the lines its API holds and the file does not yet (nearly all dated Jul to Sep 2026): 80 for Anthropic, 21 for Nvidia. For 8 more lines the API's later filing replaces the file's copy. Nine Anthropic lines to Banks for Senate are counted from a copy of the committee's report saved in Sep 2026: its amended report leaves the employer blank. No earlier copy exists for Nvidia, so a Nvidia line blanked that way is missed. Sums are of positive receipt lines, in whole dollars as the FEC's bulk file gives them. Negative lines on the same committees (refunds and chargebacks: 3 for Anthropic, $4,287; 4 for Nvidia, $200) are listed with the tables and not taken off; among the members drawn, $3,500 returned by a committee of Sen. John Cornyn. A person is counted by surname and first given name; in six of the counts a name occurs with a second spelling or ZIP code, which shows neither two people nor one, and the count stays as the rule gives it. A lobbying report names a bill; it does not say which office was visited or what was asked. Fellows, advisers and former staff are as the programme's, the group's or Congress's own pages list them. A lobbyists' line names the clients that the lobbying reports held here list for the givers' firms. The reports give each gift as the lobbyist's own money; they do not show whether a client asked for it. Whether the firm had the client when the gift was made is taken from the firm's registration dates, which the published table gives beside each gift. Why each client is on this map: Open Philanthropy's awards on record include $3.4M to Americans for Responsible Innovation (2024–25), $12.5M to the Center for AI Safety (2022–23) and $1.9M to the Future of Life Institute (2015–20), and its action fund gave IFP Action $2.0M (2022–23). The grants on record to the Center for AI Safety's action fund and to Encode AI are from Jaan Tallinn, and the Future of Life Institute gave Encode $250,000 in 2024; no Open Philanthropy award to either is on record, and none of any kind to Fathom. Nvidia registered its own political committee on Aug 27, 2026; its one report on file, through Sep 30, shows no contribution to any candidate. The same record was then pulled for both companies: the lobbyists' contribution reports for 2020 to 2026 of all 33 firms registered for Nvidia, for Anthropic or for one of the groups above. To the 27 members drawn, in gifts of Feb 2021 to Jun 2026 made while the firm was registered for the client, lobbyists listed for the client gave $70,469 on Nvidia's side, $78,500 on Anthropic's and $85,491 on the groups' side; counting every lobbyist at those firms, $429,735, $124,500 and $295,629. A firm registered for two clients puts one gift on two sides, so the sides are not added up. Each member's row gives its lines from this table by the same rule for each side: every gift of a lobbyist at a firm then registered for the client, and how much of it came from lobbyists listed for that client. Only a lobbyist's own money is counted. The reports also list contributions of political committees (a firm's PAC, a PAC a lobbyist serves, a campaign committee): 55 such lines, 28 gifts once those listed by several lobbyists of one firm are counted once, are in the table and in no sum here; until Nov 16, 2026 they were counted as lobbyists' own money. The table is published with the figure. For the Speaker and for Sen. Kennedy, who share a surname with other members, only a gift whose report gives the office is counted; for Sen. Scott, whose surname several other politicians carry, only one whose report gives his given name or its initial. What the record does not show: who gave the intelligence assessment to reporters; whether it is correct; any contact about these reports between Anthropic, or anyone tied to it, and the reporters or their sources; any contact with a member of Congress about these reports or about what the member then said or did (earlier public contacts, such as testimony at a hearing, are drawn at left). The saved reports state limits of their own: the Times's first report says officials "did not believe" Huang knew the woman was gathering information when the president was first briefed, and that Huang "has not received a defensive briefing"; Nvidia said its customers get "zero information relevant to national security", and the Times reports its spokesman saying that customers do not ask Nvidia to press the U.S. government to change its policies on chip sales to China. That first report also says it "could not be determined which intelligence agency or agencies" monitored her, and that it is not clear what information she passed along or what it was worth to China. NBC reports that the president, asked whether he was briefed before he took Huang to China in May, said "I didn't hear about it then" and later "They could have been mentioned." Nvidia's side, the same classes of record: its employees' gifts are drawn beside Anthropic's; its political committee is new and has given to no candidate; its lobbyists' gifts are counted above with Anthropic's and the groups'; bills named in its lobbying reports are drawn; past posts with a drawn member that its lobbyists declare are drawn (Banks, Kennedy, McCaul), as is the one found for a lobbyist of Anthropic (Thune). Its support of institutions whose people are drawn is worded in their rows (CSET, CNAS, the Council on Foreign Relations); the donor lists of Brookings and 80,000 Hours do not name it, and a reader from another model family found it on none of the lists that IAPS, the Foundation for American Innovation, the Institute for Progress and the Tarbell Center publish, most of which are partial. Quoted people with a past post at Nvidia or paid work for it are drawn (Moorhead, Newman, Boloor, Yoo; both companies support Barez's research), and business with Nvidia that a saved page states is worded for two public voices (Musk, Delangue). Looked for and not established: a witness from Nvidia before these members' committees, advertising aimed at their districts, a seat on their advisory bodies. Those searches have gaps: the ad libraries could not be read, the search of the records held ended with 3,839 hits unread, and the web search left 491 targets unopened. The map still starts from Anthropic and Open Philanthropy at the left of each slice, so the number of lines says nothing about either company's influence. The Times's and the FT's reports are cited from their own articles, saved by hand; the Journal's own site turns away automated readers: its report of Oct 30 is cited from its own page, saved by hand, and from the copy a licensed partner carries (Tiger Brokers), its report of Nov 11 from a partner's copy (the Greek paper To Vima). An earlier report that a paper attributed to an Anthropic executive is drawn as a tie in that paper's row: one is on record, the FT's of Sep 2025, known here through another outlet's account of it, which does not say whether the FT alone had it. The papers' earlier reporting was not searched for others, and reports attributed to Nvidia executives were not looked up. The own channel (official site, newsroom, own feed or account) of each of the 82 actors who had spoken was searched once for these fifteen days by a reader from another model family: on Nov 14 for the 63 then drawn, on Nov 15 for the 14 added since and then for the three members and the two others drawn later that day (the two share-price rows have none; one voice among the 82 is no longer drawn). An item about the affair is held and was read for 41 (the three papers among them, through articles saved by hand); for two links were located and none could be saved (Anthropic's SEC filings, a page of OpenAI's); four had only items that do not mention the affair or are not their own; for 25 a channel that could be read showed no item about the affair in these fifteen days; for 10 no channel could be read. An item is counted only where the project holds the page, and a share-sale filing or policy paper that a chip draws as context is not counted as an item about the affair. The reader could open no account on X in either round, and a channel with nothing found is not proof of silence. Of the 133 chips drawn before those searches, the original was read and is now cited for 36; for seven more the search did not yield the original, but a saved copy of the publisher's page is now cited (one of them shows only the opening); for nine more the reader could not open a post on X, and the post itself, saved afterwards by its id, is now cited; for one it carries the first of the chip's two remarks; for 71 it still could not be opened (posts on X and Truth Social, broadcasters' video, papers behind a paywall); for two the reader found it and the site refused the project's own copy (the Journal's page, an SEC filing); and for 7 it was not found. Of the chips still without their original, 14 now also cite a paper's own report of the act, from the papers' pages saved since the first census. The 54 chips added without such a search each cite the actor's own page, the paper's own article (some in a licensed copy) or, where neither is held, a report that the chip names. Source: 2,254 links from saved aggregator pages; saved reports, posts and releases; committee filings; rows held in the congress, lineage, toner and evaluators packs. Aggregator pages for Oct 29 to Nov 12 were retrieved on Nov 12 and Nov 14, 2026; other sources were saved Nov 12 to 15, 2026; rows of the packs carry their own earlier dates. Status: draft of Nov 16, 2026. Each passage behind a drawn item was matched by script to a saved copy of its source. Fourteen independent readings by another company's model have read the figure or the corrections made to it. The first (Nov 14) read the 230 rows then drawn that are not listed pieces, recounted the pieces and recomputed the members' lines. The second (Nov 15), in three parts, read the 168 rows new or changed since then, the figure element by element, the pieces and the money recounted from the FEC's saved records, and who is drawn and what the chips carry; it graded 11 points as errors and 145 as needing a qualification. The third (Nov 15) read the corrections made in answer: it found no error in the 90 changed rows, two errors and eight qualifications in the changed text, and held 2 of the 181 answers insufficient and 19 only in part. A fourth (Nov 15) read the answers to it and the 45 rows added or changed since: no error in a row, 24 qualifications (18 of them one point, that lobbyists' gifts were shown by unequal measures), two errors and nine qualifications in the changed text, and 13 of 51 answers held only in part. A fifth (Nov 15) read the answers to that: no problem in the 44 rows it read, four points on the wording of the notes, and 48 of 49 answers held. The most serious points across the first six: a PAC gift that was recorded and not drawn; joint committees tied to a member before their statements were read; look-ups that had missed records the tables hold, three banks among them; chips that left out a clause qualifying what was said; and people left out by a rule that was not applied alike to both companies. Each finding has a written disposition, published with the tables. No reading fetched the originals again. A sixth (Nov 15) graded the answers to the fifth and found them right but for one sentence of the notes, which now stands in the wording that reading proposed. A seventh (Nov 15) read the 67 rows added or changed after the sixth and the new counting of articles: 62 rows ok, five needing a qualification, none in error; it found the counting of articles unsound (10 of 25 joined pairs it sampled were different works, four of 15 unjoined pairs the same; dates read from headers a day off; one senator drawn on three articles that are two reports). An eighth (Nov 16) read the answers to that: the ten changed rows ok and 59 of 66 answers holding, but the count of articles still not reliable (wire copies not joined, five articles left out although their saved pages hold them, two empty pages counted), and summaries that still counted a senator withdrawn in that release. In answer a third reader opened every pair of pages that share a fifth of their text, the article text of 25 pages was taken again from the saved pages, that senator (Scott) is drawn again and another (Warner) no longer rests on a reader's comment, each on a third report saved since, and 54 more pages saved by hand on Nov 16 were read and counted. A ninth (Nov 16) read both of those rounds: nine of the ten changed rows ok and 63 of 72 answers holding; one member's line counted a political committee's contribution as a lobbyist's own money, a company filing's event date had been taken for its day of publication, and three of the re-extracted pages still lacked a paragraph. In answer the fault in the lobbyists' lines was looked for in every member's and found in 54 lines, the chips on the resignation and the appointments were given the filing's dates, and four pages were taken again and read again. A tenth (Nov 16) read those answers: the 17 changed rows ok and all 54 answers holding, 12 of them in part; one line of committee money had still been missed (a campaign committee whose name holds the lobbyist's surname), one representative's count of articles was two short, and two sentences claimed too much (how many headlines name people who are not drawn; that an independent reader judged every pair of pages). In answer a contribution counts as a lobbyist's own only when the report says SELF or gives the filer's name and nothing else, which corrected one more member's line (the groups' side is $295,629; it was $391,629 before the ninth reading), and that representative is counted under his legal given name too. An eleventh (Nov 16) read those answers and the same corrections in the three-chairmen figure: all 46 answers hold, and it found no misclassified line of money among the 193 of 678 lines it read, the rule run on all 678 agreeing. It found one counted page that is a subscription preview and was not marked as held in part, a sentence in a supporting table saying that no client directed the lobbyists' gifts, which the reports do not show, the names searched for some members lacking a form the roster gives, and this note's count of readings out of date. In answer a reader went through the 248 counted pages that show a sign of a barrier or hold a short text, which raised the pages marked as held only in part from 58 to 92; a table and five photo captions that the extraction had left out were added to the text read, which raised four members' counts of articles (Mast 91, Moolenaar 78, Crawford 68, the Speaker 10); the given name or its usual short form was added to the names searched for eleven members, changing no count; and the supporting table's sentence was replaced. A twelfth (Nov 16) read those answers and the interactive map made from the figure: every member's count, the added passages and the money reproduce, and 37 of 40 answers hold, three in part. It found, on the interactive map, members' lines shown without their sources, searches that found nothing counted as ties, and a label claiming a current post; and in the tables a complete newsletter marked as held in part while one cut off by its paywall was not, a live page with collapsed entries not marked, lines of prose dropped at the page breaks of a page saved by hand as PDF, and photo captions missing from the text read. It closed incomplete: four hand-saved PDFs could not be opened where it ran. In answer the interactive map lists every source, sets the empty searches apart and is relabelled; 93 pages were marked as held only in part, under the stated rule that a page is whole when all of its own piece is saved; 21 dropped lines were put back on four pages and two pages trimmed of a following article's opening lines; and the missing captions were stated as a limit. A thirteenth (Nov 16) read those answers and opened the four PDFs: 72 of 83 answers hold and 11 hold in part; every restored line and both trims are right, and the stated limit on captions is enough for the counts. It found a second newsletter that stops at its own paywall and was not marked; three things about live pages (one whose saved HTML holds 143 entries, of which the text read held 21; one that holds 69, of which 20 were read; and four copies of one live page that hold only its latest entries and were not marked); the three-chairmen figure counting two posts from a text since replaced; and the search for collapse marks described as wider than it was. It closed incomplete: two source views were not available to it. In answer 172 entries were added to the text read of three live pages, which raised eight members' counts by one or two (Warren 71, Coons 48, Jeffries 30, Schumer 22, Thune 13, Johnson 11, Cornyn 9, Mast 92); 98 pages were marked as held only in part; every counted page with any collapse mark was read, and every saved page with a live-blog record was compared with its text; a census reader read the three live pages again for remarks; and the three-chairmen figure was made to read the same text as this one (93, 81 and 74 pages). A fourteenth (Nov 16) read those answers: every count reproduces, 36 of 43 answers hold and seven hold in part, and it would keep the rule that counts a live page of general news like any article, with the four members it names only for other news marked more plainly. It found two acts in the new census reading that no chip carried (a representative's remark of Nov 12 and a reported Justice Department inquiry), a letter's signature and two summary bullets still missing from two live pages, and four sentences that said too much or dated a search to one day. It closed incomplete: whether one live page saved as PDF had older entries cannot be settled from the PDF. Changed in answer and not yet read independently: the two acts are drawn, and a second gauge over every drawn actor and day found six more acts that two or more articles report in different words and no chip carried (among them the attorney general's statement of Nov 12 that the department had reached no conclusions about the woman in the reports); eight acts are added in all; one older act moved from its report's day to its own, and one chip's dashed edge became solid. The four members are marked beside their counts; the small parts are added; the sentences are corrected. After that release the builder read what its own gauges had left unread, and no independent reader has read the result: the 31 days on which only one counted article carries an actor who has no chip that day, and, with a third gauge, the quoted remarks that two or more articles carry in differing words and no chip held. Thirteen more acts are drawn (among them the president's answer of Nov 12 that it was not yet determined whether the woman was a spy, Nvidia's and the Chinese embassy's replies to the Times report of Nov 6, and who backed the export controls at the meeting of Nov 5), and two chips that printed half of a remark now print both halves. A fifteenth reading is under way on the release before these additions.
